title: Amateur astronomers use AI to comb through 19 million stars: potential exoplanet signals identified, handed to professional team for verification

content_html:
With AI "working the night shift" on telescope data, amateur enthusiasts can also reach the threshold of professional discovery. In a blog post published on November 24, OpenAI said that two amateur researchers, using Codex and Astra, found multiple potential exoplanet signals in public telescope data and submitted them to professional astronomers for independent verification—although they have not been officially confirmed, they are already leads worth following up on.

First, Practice on Known Answers

OpenAI engineer Kevin Bond first used Codex to systematically screen about 100,000 stars observed by the Kepler telescope, and from more than 200 candidate signals, he re-identified 10 confirmed planet signals—essentially giving the method an "open-book exam." Two astronomers from NASA's TESS mission research institute then independently reviewed the results and also homed in on two of the signals: a star in Lyra dims regularly every 13.8 days; if it is indeed a planetary transit, its diameter would be about 2.4 times that of Earth. The other signal has a period of 4.8 days, and the planet could be smaller than Neptune.

Panning for Gold Among 19 Million Stars

The other researcher went further—Ethan Byrd, founder of the startup Primitive, used Astra to scan TESS and other public observation data covering about 19 million stars, identifying 49 candidate targets. The most promising one has been submitted to NASA's TESS team for analysis. This type of search relies on the "transit method": when a planet passes in front of its host star, it blocks a sliver of starlight, causing the brightness to dip slightly and periodically. AI helps build the search pipeline and fish out signals missed by traditional algorithms from massive amounts of light-curve data.
